transcript:
Meeting header: Date: 2025-10-20 16:00 PDT, Duration: ~62 minutes. Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), Kathy Morales (Nimbus - Head of ML), Ravi Singh (Nimbus - Infra), Jon Park (Nimbus - SRE).

Summary: Technical deep dive focused on throughput limits and behavior under cold KV-cache conditions, adaptive-window batching approaches (we use 'adaptive-windowing' to mean dynamic batching window based on queue length + latency SLO), scheduler knobs (max_num_seqs, token caps, schedule_epoch_ms), and quantization tradeoffs. Customer is evaluating Dedicated + VPC pilot to handle peak routing for routing/tracking prompts with spiky burst patterns.

Topics: roofline analysis, cold vs warmed KV cache, adaptive batching/windowing heuristics, max_num_seqs and token_limit interactions, sequence packing, int8/int4 quantization impact on GPU memory and latency, VPC network egress and KMS for encryption, pilot plan and success criteria.

[00:00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick check — audio ok?
[00:00:04] Kathy Morales: Yep, good here.
[00:00:07] Priya Patel: audio's fine. We've got about an hour — thanks for the agenda, Kathy.
[00:00:15] Alex Chen: Great. The plan today: Priya'll run through the roofline-style benchmarks and show some cold-cache vs warmed-cache curves, then we can dig into scheduler knobs and tradeoffs, and finish with pilot logistics. Sound good?
[00:00:26] Kathy Morales: Sounds great. Our main concern is making sure our tracking pipeline survives the morning spikes — we're latency-sensitive for the front-end dashboards.

[00:00:34] Priya Patel: Cool — quick context: Redwood's scheduler has a few levers we tune: max_num_seqs (max concurrent sequences in a batch), token_limit (per-request token cap), scheduling window (how long we wait to build a batch), and priority buckets. Adaptive-windowing is our approach where window length shrinks/grows based on current queue length and observed tail latency.

[00:01:02] Ravi Singh: Quick Q: when you say "cold KV cache" do you mean the KV cache hasn't been populated for a specific user or prompt prefix? We saw a 3x throughput drop in our internal run when we started from cold.
[00:01:13] Priya Patel: Yeah, cold means the per-session KV cache is empty — first requests don't get the hit-rate we expect. That affects both memory access and batching patterns — more tokens are recomputed or fetched from remote storage depending on the config.

[00:01:28] Jon Park: Also we saw the scheduler send a lot of 1-item batches during spikes — that killed TPU/GPU efficiency.
[00:01:34] Priya Patel: Right — that's the classic tradeoff: small batches -> lower latency for single requests but worse token/sec throughput. Adaptive-windowing tries to avoid that by allowing aggressive packing during bursts but respecting tail SLOs.

[00:01:50] [00:02:00] Priya Patel: I have a short screen share with a few roofline plots — I'll describe them verbally since Fireflies might not capture the images. The X axis is sequences-per-batch, Y is tokens/sec. We run three curves: cold KV cache, warm KV cache, and warm + high packing (max_num_seqs bumped).
[00:02:15] Priya Patel: Key point: with cold cache and default quant (fp16), tokens/sec tops out much lower, because more memory traffic and de/sync overhead. When we warm the KV cache, tokens/sec increases by roughly 1.8x on the same instance type. If we then increase max_num_seqs to push packing, tokens/sec can improve another 1.3x, but latency tail increases if scheduling window is too long.

[00:02:43] Kathy Morales: So you're saying it's not just a single knob. We can't only increase max_num_seqs because we'll blow the 99th percentile latency.
[00:02:50] Priya Patel: Exactly. You tune max_num_seqs together with a bounded scheduling window and a token_limit. For example, one strategy we recommend: set max_num_seqs to something like 24 for a 48GB GPU model with 2k typical seq len, set token_limit to 512 for interactive endpoints, and use an adaptive window that starts at 10ms and expands to 60ms when queue depth grows. That keeps P50 low and gains throughput on the P95 tradeoff curve.

[00:03:18] Ravi Singh: Those numbers — 24 sequences on a 48GB card — do you have sample math for memory headroom when using int8 vs fp16? We're evaluating int8 quantization for Dedicated hosts.
[00:03:27] Priya Patel: Yeah — int8 reduces model memory by ~2.5-3x depending on operator coverage. That gives you more headroom for kv cache + more concurrent seqs. But there's a latency delta: int8 can sometimes add ~5-15% per-token latency on some ops depending on kernel availability; in other cases it reduces latency due to better memory bandwidth. We provided a short quant recommendation doc in the onboarding folder — I'll reshare.

[00:03:50] Alex Chen: Quick clarification — when we say "roofline" we're looking at compute-bound vs memory-bound regimes. Cold KV cache tends to move you into memory-bound because of cache misses and backend fetches. Warm cache is more compute bound and leverages batching well.

[00:04:05] Kathy Morales: That matches our observation. Any quick mitigation for cold-cache spikes other than pre-warming?
[00:04:11] Priya Patel: A few options: pre-warm during onboarding by replaying representative prompts, keep a hot-set of common prefixes in the shared KV cache, or enable a small warm-cache policy where we accept slightly longer-lived KV entries for heavy users. Also at the scheduler level, allowing a short initial buffering window (e.g., 30ms) can let the first few requests aggregate and populate cache faster.

[00:04:33] Jon Park: Is there a way to prioritize warm-hit traffic so it doesn't get stuck behind cold-heavy batches?
[00:04:38] Priya Patel: Yes — Redwood supports priority buckets. You can tag requests with a priority label; the scheduler will try to co-locate similar priorities and prefer batches that maximize hit-rate. That requires the client (or your routing layer) to mark cold-user requests differently, or we can infer based on TTL.

[00:04:54] [00:05:00] Ravi Singh: About scheduler knobs: you mentioned schedule_epoch_ms earlier — can you explain how that interacts with adaptive-windowing?
[00:05:07] Priya Patel: schedule_epoch_ms is the heartbeat the scheduler uses to evaluate whether to flush a batch. In adaptive-windowing we dynamically adjust the per-epoch aggregation target: if queue depth is low, epoch ms is low (e.g., 5-10ms); if queue depth spikes, epoch ms can grow up to a configured max (say 50-80ms) to let more sequences pack. The control loop uses observed latency and queue length.

[00:05:34] Alex Chen: We also have a safety guard — a hard token cap per batch so a single long request doesn't delay others. That's the token_limit parameter.

[00:05:42] Kathy Morales: For our use case most requests are short (avg 60 tokens), but we have occasional long trace generation up to 1.2k tokens. How do you prevent those from skewing scheduling?
[00:05:51] Priya Patel: Two approaches: 1) set token_limit to e.g., 512 for the interactive route so any >512 request is routed to a different route or throttled, or 2) enable splitting where long requests are processed in their own dedicated batch (you can tag them). That depends on acceptable UX for those long jobs.

[00:06:08] Jon Park: Okay. What about quantization and inference kernels — you said int4 is promising but patchy kernel support?
[00:06:14] Priya Patel: Correct. int4 gives big memory wins but kernel support across op types is inconsistent. We use a hybrid approach: quantize matmul weights aggressively and keep some attention kernels in int8 or fp16 when int4 kernels aren't stable. The backend will fallback to a compatible path. We test fallbacks extensively because falling back at runtime can cause latency spikes if not warmed.

[00:06:33] Kathy Morales: Does Redwood expose a knob to prefer "no fallback" to avoid runtime surprises?
[00:06:38] Priya Patel: Yes, you can pin a quantization profile and mark it "strict" — that will reject deployment if all kernels aren't available on the target hardware. Useful for predictable latency but more conservative.

[00:06:50] [00:07:00] Ravi Singh: Network/perf related: since we'll be in a VPC, does KV cache access happen inside customer VPC or traverse Redwood control plane? We need to know data residency and egress implications.
[00:07:09] Alex Chen: For Redwood Private deployments, the KV cache can be colocated inside your VPC or on-prem — it does not go through our control plane. For Hosted, cache is in Redwood-managed infra (we can enable customer-managed encryption keys for at-rest). We'll share a tech note.

[00:07:23] Ravi Singh: Good. KMS integration — do you support customer-supplied HSM keys?
[00:07:27] Priya Patel: Yes, for Private we integrate with AWS KMS and on-prem HSMs. We'll need the contact for your security team to exchange requirements.

[00:07:36] Kathy Morales: Back to throughput: can you walk through a sample run where you change max_num_seqs and show the latency distributions?

[00:07:43] Priya Patel: Sure. Example run (48GB A100 equiv): baseline default config (max_num_seqs=12, schedule window=15ms) -> P50 18ms, P95 72ms, tokens/sec ~220k. Increase max_num_seqs to 24 and expand window to 50ms -> P50 23ms, P95 140ms, tokens/sec ~330k. If we then apply warm KV cache (prewarmed prefixes) tokens/sec goes to ~380k and P95 drops to 110ms. So you see throughput gains but tail latency shifts. That's where adaptive-windowing tries to find the knee.

[00:08:20] Jon Park: Those P95 numbers are a bit high for our dashboard. We need P95 < 100ms ideally. Is there a middle ground?

[00:08:25] Priya Patel: Yes — you can use a mixed routing strategy: keep your interactive endpoint conservative (max_num_seqs=12) to hit P95 <100ms for dashboard traffic and route batch/analytics traffic to a Dedicated pool tuned for high throughput. Another trick is to set priority buckets and let the scheduler prefer low-latency buckets when load is close to SLO threshold.

[00:08:43] Kathy Morales: Wouldn't that require duplicate capacity? We're mindful of cost.

[00:08:47] Alex Chen: We often do a hybrid: small Dedicated footprint for the low-latency front-end, and a larger shared pool for heavier workloads. Redwood Optimize suggests quant and batching profiles based on your workload to reduce the Dedicated size. Also burst capacity can help during spikes without full-time Reserved capacity.

[00:09:02] Ravi Singh: Pricing aside, for the pilot we want to validate these knobs end-to-end. What's the minimal pilot to exercise cold-cache spikes and warm steady-state?

[00:09:10] Priya Patel: A 48-72 hour pilot with: representative traffic replay (including morning spike), prewarming scripts for hot prefixes, toggles for quant profiles (fp16/int8), and a control variant with default scheduler knobs. We'll collect P50/P95/P99 and trace KV hit rates, memory headroom, and GPU perf counters. That should reveal the roofline knee.

[00:09:28] Kathy Morales: Sounds good. We'll prepare a traffic replay — one question: are there out-of-the-box dashboards in the Console for KV hit rate and batch composition?

[00:09:36] Priya Patel: Yes — Redwood Console exposes token-level breakdowns, KV hit-rate over time, batch composition (avg seqs per batch), and kernel fallback alerts. We'll make a tailored dashboard for the pilot.

[00:09:49] [00:10:00] Alex Chen: Let me call out a few real-world heuristics we've seen: - For interactive endpoints with spiky traffic, set a conservative max_num_seqs but enable burst capacity so you can handle sudden surges. - For model families that support quant well, use int8 to reduce Dedicated footprint. - Try a short artificial queueing window (20-40ms) during ingress to increase packing without impacting P95 much.

[00:10:22] Ravi Singh: Artificial queueing window — does that mean we buffer requests in our ingress layer or Redwood will buffer?

[00:10:27] Priya Patel: Redwood's ingress can buffer; you can also do it in your sidecar. We recommend Redwood buffering because it ties into the scheduler's knowledge of queue depth and priority buckets.

[00:10:36] Jon Park: In our security review we saw that headers can include priority tags — is that how you suggest tagging?

[00:10:40] Priya Patel: Exactly — include X-Redwood-Priority or similar header (we'll share the exact header names) so we can keep warm hits prioritized.

[00:10:47] Kathy Morales: Any gotchas around sequence packing with conversation state? We have per-user prefixes and we don't want cross-user contamination.

[00:10:53] Priya Patel: Redwood never mixes KV state across sessions. Sequence packing is purely about token-level packing for GPU efficiency; each sequence keeps its own KV context. That said, packing sequences with vastly different lengths can waste padding tokens — consider length-binning as a pre-batching step (we support it).

[00:11:09] Alex Chen: Also note the max_num_seqs interacts with KV memory: more sequences = more KV entries in memory for that batch; ensure your instance type has headroom. We'll provide a calculator.

[00:11:18] Ravi Singh: Perfect. A few administrative questions: SOC2 and audit logs — we need proof for procurement.

[00:11:24] Alex Chen: We are SOC 2 Type II certified; we can send the attestation and our SOC2 report redacted. Audit logs are available in the Console for Private and Dedicated with configurable retention.

[00:11:34] Kathy Morales: Great. Any last deep-dive point we should consider?

[00:11:38] Priya Patel: One more: cold-cache warmup cost. Pre-warming is effective but has a cost because you consume tokens. A targeted strategy — warm only hot prefixes and use a probabilistic prefetch for long-tail prefixes — often gives best ROI. We'll include a small script that samples your prompt set and suggests the top K prefixes to warm.

[00:11:58] [00:12:00] Kathy Morales: That would be helpful.

[00:12:03] Alex Chen: Ok let's move to wrap up — recap and next steps.

Recap: Redwood showed roofline-style benchmarks highlighting cold vs warm KV cache differences, explained adaptive-windowing and how schedule_epoch_ms + max_num_seqs + token_limit interact, discussed quantization tradeoffs (fp16/int8/int4) and kernel fallback risks, covered VPC/KMS behavior for Private deployment, and outlined the pilot plan.

Next steps (as discussed):
- Priya will share the roofline benchmark script, quant recommendation doc, and header naming for priority tagging by 2025-10-22.
- Nimbus (Ravi/Kathy) to provide representative prompt set, traffic histogram, and SSO/KMS contacts by 2025-10-24.
- Redwood (Alex) to send draft Dedicated burst pricing and pilot terms by 2025-10-23.
- Schedule follow-up pilot review for week of 2025-11-03 (tentative).

[00:12:58] Kathy Morales: Thanks everyone. This was useful — looking forward to the scripts.
[00:13:04] Alex Chen: Thanks — we'll follow up in email with links to the onboarding folder and the pilot runbook.
[00:13:08] Ravi Singh: Appreciate it. Bye.

End of transcript.
